title: Grammar Map · All 15 patterns in one listen (the boy and the moon)
summary: A one-off: the gist of all fifteen Latin patterns from the app's Forms > Patterns ladder, one focus pyramid each, through a small boy learning to ask about everything, and his dad. Who (quī), when, because, if, although (Quamquam domum īre voluit, tamen laetus lūsit), says that (Dīcit lūnam nōs sequī), so that, asking, the participle, the ablative absolute, cum + subjunctive, the hidden question (Scīre vult cūr lūna nōs sequātur), result, the gerund, and -ndum est. Then the whole map in one evening, and the Latin alone twice. Iulia's voice.
lines: {Salvē!} This is a special episode. The Grammar Map. All fifteen patterns in one listen. Just the gist of each, with one focus idea.
Our world today: a small boy who is learning to ask for things and to ask about everything. I am his dad. He is my son, {fīlius meus}.
First, the asking kit. Short lines a small child uses all day long.
Small words, big ideas. Now the fifteen patterns.
Pattern one. Who and which. {Quī} adds a mini-sentence about a noun.
The boy who asks about everything is my son.
Puer quī omnia rogat fīlius meus est.
The boy who always says why...
The boy who always says why is my son.
Puer quī semper Cūr dīcit fīlius meus est.
Why? Because he wants to know.
Spot it: a noun, then {quī}, {quae} or {quod}. Read: who, or which. Careful: {quod} can also mean because.
Puer quī omnia rogat fīlius meus est.
The boy who asks about everything is my son.
Pattern two. When. {Cum}, {ubi} and {postquam} tell you when something happens.
He sees the moon. He says hello to it.
When he sees the moon, he says hello to it.
When he sees the moon, he says: hello, moon!
Cum lūnam videt, dīcit: Salvē, lūna!
When we come to the park, he runs to the big tree.
Ubi in hortum venīmus, ad arborem magnam currit.
After we came home, he looked for the moon again.
Postquam domum vēnimus, lūnam iterum quaesīvit.
Spot it: {cum}, {ubi} or {postquam}, a mini-sentence, then a comma.
When he sees the moon, he says hello to it.
Pattern three. Because. {Quod} or {quia} gives the reason.
He wants to go home because...
He wants to go home because he wants to see Mum.
Domum īre vult quod Mātrem vidēre vult.
He is glad because the moon is here.
He is glad because the moon is here again.
Spot it: {quod} or {quia} plus a normal verb. Read: because.
Domum īre vult quod Mātrem vidēre vult.
He wants to go home because he wants to see Mum.
Pattern four. If and unless. {Sī} means if. {Nisi} means unless.
We have time. We play again.
If we have time, we play again.
If it does not rain, we go to the park.
Sī pluvia nōn cadit, in hortum īmus.
If the moon is there, he says hello to it.
Unless it rains, we play outside.
Spot it: {sī} or {nisi} at the start, a comma after the mini-sentence.
If we have time, we play again.
Pattern five. Although. {Quamquam}, and often {tamen}: still.
Although he wanted to go home...
Although he wanted to go home, he played happily.
Quamquam domum īre voluit, laetus lūsit.
Although he wanted to go home, he still played happily.
Quamquam domum īre voluit, tamen laetus lūsit.
Although he is small, he understands many things.
Spot it: {quamquam} at the start, often {tamen} after.
Quamquam domum īre voluit, tamen laetus lūsit.
Although he wanted to go home, he still played happily.
Pattern six. Says that. No word for that. The person or thing goes into the object form, the verb into the infinitive.
My son says that the moon follows us.
Fīlius meus dīcit lūnam nōs sequī.
My son thinks that the moon...
My son thinks that the moon is his friend.
Fīlius meus putat lūnam amīcam suam esse.
He says that the trees are sleeping.
{Sequitur} became {sequī}. {Est} became {esse}. Spot it: a say or think verb, the object form, an infinitive. Read: that.
Fīlius meus dīcit lūnam nōs sequī.
My son says that the moon follows us.
Pattern seven. So that. {Ut}, and for so that not, {nē}. The verb takes the swapped form: {videt} becomes {videat}.
He climbs onto the chair. He sees everything.
He climbs onto the chair so that he sees everything.
In sellam ascendit ut omnia videat.
He opens the window so that he sees the moon.
He calls me so that I see the moon too.
Mē vocat ut ego quoque lūnam videam.
We walk slowly so that we do not fall.
Spot it: {ut} or {nē}, then the swapped verb. Read: so that, or so that not.
In sellam ascendit ut omnia videat.
He climbs onto the chair so that he sees everything.
Pattern eight. Asking and ordering. After ask, beg or order: {ut} means to, {nē} means not to.
He asks me to play again.
He begs me to tell a story.
I ask him to help me.
Spot it: an ask or order verb, a person, then {ut} or {nē}. Read: to, or not to.
He asks me to play again.
Pattern nine. The participle. A verb used like a describing word. Like {currēns}: running, at the same time as the main verb. You'll meet this properly later.
My son runs. He comes to me.
Fīlius meus currit. Ad mē venit.
My son comes running to me.
Fīlius meus currēns ad mē venit.
My son, watching the moon, is silent.
Spot it: a verb like {currēns} or {spectāns} next to a person. Read: while doing it.
Fīlius meus currēns ad mē venit.
My son comes running to me.

Pattern ten. The ablative absolute. A little side scene, set apart: with this happening, that happens. Both words go into the with-form. The verb word often ends like {cadente}. You'll meet this properly later.
The moon shines. My son plays.
While the moon shines, my son plays.
With the sun setting, we look for the moon.
With the sun setting, we look for the moon together.
Spot it: two words at the start, set off by a comma, like {sōle cadente}. Read: while, or with.
With the sun setting, we look for the moon together.

Pattern eleven. {Cum} in a past story, with a new verb form: when, or since. It looks like the whole infinitive plus an ending. {Esse} becomes {esset}. {Vidēre} becomes {vidēret}. You'll meet this properly later.
We were in the park. He saw the moon.
When we were in the park, he saw the moon.
Cum in hortō essēmus, lūnam vīdit.
When he saw the moon, he said: look!
When he saw the moon, he said: look, Dad, the moon is following us!
Cum lūnam vidēret, dīxit: Ecce, Pater, lūna nōs sequitur!
Spot it: {cum} plus a verb built on the infinitive, like {vidēret}. Read: when, or since, in a story.
When he saw the moon, he said: look!
Pattern twelve. The hidden question. A question inside a sentence. Its verb takes the swapped form.
Why does the moon follow us?
He wants to know why the moon follows us.
Scīre vult cūr lūna nōs sequātur.
He asks where the moon sleeps.
I don't know where the moon sleeps.
{Sequitur} became {sequātur}. {Dormit} became {dormiat}. Spot it: know or ask, then a question word, then a swapped verb.
Scīre vult cūr lūna nōs sequātur.
He wants to know why the moon follows us.
Pattern thirteen. Result. So much that. Look for {tam} or {ita} first, then {ut}.
He is so eager that he gets up at once.
Tam cupidus est ut statim surgat.
He asks so many things that I learn too.
Tam multa rogat ut ego quoque discam.
It's true. I learn a lot.
Spot it: {tam} or {ita} early, then {ut}. Read: so much that. No {tam} or {ita}? Then {ut} usually means so that, or to.
Tam multa rogat ut ego quoque discam.
He asks so many things that I learn too.
Pattern fourteen. The gerund. A verb used like a noun: playing, asking. {Lūdendī}: of playing. You'll meet this properly later.
My son is keen on playing.
He is a master of asking.
Spot it: a word like {lūdendī} or {rogandī} after time, keen or master. Read: of doing it.
My son is keen on playing.
Pattern fifteen. Must. {Dormiendum est}: sleeping must be done. Short, strong, and very useful.
Now we must sleep. But first I tell a story.
Nunc dormiendum est. Sed prīmum fābulam nārrō.
Two ways to say must. {Dēbēs}, an ordinary verb. And {dormiendum est}: it has to be done. Who does it? The story tells you.
Nunc dormiendum est. Sed prīmum fābulam nārrō.
Now we must sleep. But first I tell a story.
The whole map, in one short evening. Fifteen patterns.
The boy who asks about everything is my son.
Puer quī omnia rogat fīlius meus est.
When we come to the park, he runs to the big tree.
Ubi in hortum venīmus, ad arborem magnam currit.
If we have time, we play again.
With the sun setting, we look for the moon together.
My son, watching the moon, is silent.
He says that the moon follows us.
He wants to know why the moon follows us.
Scīre vult cūr lūna nōs sequātur.
Then he wants to go home, because he wants to see Mum.
Tum domum īre vult, quod Mātrem vidēre vult.
Although he wanted to go home, he still played happily.
Quamquam domum īre voluit, tamen laetus lūsit.
At home he climbs onto the chair so that he sees the moon.
Domī in sellam ascendit ut lūnam videat.
When he saw the moon, he said: look, it followed us!
Cum lūnam vidēret, dīxit: Ecce, nōs secūta est!
He asks me to tell a story.
He asks so many things that I learn too.
Tam multa rogat ut ego quoque discam.
He is keen on playing, and keen on asking.
Cupidus lūdendī est, et cupidus rogandī.
Now we must sleep. But first I tell a story.
Nunc dormiendum est. Sed prīmum fābulam nārrō.
That is the map. Fifteen patterns. You don't need them all yet. Now you know the shape of each one. {Valē!} Now the Latin alone, twice.
